claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: No differences in OPC proliferation were observed between EYFP+ and EYFP– populations in either hippocampus or corpus callosum.
claims.source: Although the proportion of BrdU+ OPCs varied by region, from ~45% in hippocampus to ~60% in corpus callosum, no differences were observed between EYFP+ and EYFP– populations in either region (Figure 3B–E; Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C), indicating comparable rates of proliferation.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of BrdU incorporation shown in Figure 3B-E.

claims.claim: No significant differences in OPC differentiation were observed between control and Kir4.1-deleted OPCs.
claims.source: At this time point, EYFP+ cells consisted of ~75% PDGFRα+ OPCs and ~15% CC1+ oligodendrocytes in the hippocampus, and ~45% OPCs and ~40% oligodendrocytes in the corpus callosum, with no significant differences observed between control and Kir4.1-deleted OPCs (Figure 3F–H; Figure 3—figure supplement 3D–F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 3F-H.

claims.claim: Depolarization and increased membrane resistance induced by Kir4.1 deletion did not alter OPC proliferation or differentiation into oligodendrocytes.
claims.source: Thus, although OPCs lacking Kir4.1 exhibited markedly higher membrane resistance and more depolarized membrane potential, remarkably, these changes did not alter their proliferation or differentiation into oligodendrocytes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Oligodendrocytes in mixed glial cultures from Kcnj10−/− mice are significantly depolarized and fail to mature fully.
claims.source: Oligodendrocytes in mixed glial cultures from Kcnj10−/− mice are significantly depolarized and fail to mature fully (Neusch et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Selective deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter their membrane properties.
claims.source: However, selective deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter their membrane properties, the structure of myelin (Figure 4), or the baseline conduction velocity of action potentials in white matter (Figure 4D; Figure 7B–C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Selective deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter the structure of myelin.
claims.source: However, selective deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter their membrane properties, the structure of myelin (Figure 4), or the baseline conduction velocity of action potentials in white matter (Figure 4D; Figure 7B–C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunostaining and TEM data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Selective deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter the baseline conduction velocity of action potentials in white matter.
claims.source: However, selective deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter their membrane properties, the structure of myelin (Figure 4), or the baseline conduction velocity of action potentials in white matter (Figure 4D; Figure 7B–C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4D and Figure 7B-C.

claims.claim: Oligodendrocytes express a variety of K+ leak channels that may compensate for the loss of Kir4.1, including K2P channels and the inward-rectifying channel Kir2.1.
claims.source: Oligodendrocytes express a variety of K+ leak channels that may compensate for the loss of Kir4.1, including K2P channels and the inward-rectifying channel Kir2.1 (Gipson and Bordey, 2002; Hawkins and Butt, 2013; Pérez-Samartín et al., 2017; Stonehouse et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Astrocytes in Kcnj10−/− mice are severely depolarized.
claims.source: Astrocytes in Kcnj10−/− mice are also severely depolarized, and their ability to remove extracellular K+ is impaired (Djukic et al., 2007), consistent with their high expression of this channel.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: The ability of astrocytes to remove extracellular K+ is impaired in Kcnj10−/− mice.
claims.source: Astrocytes in Kcnj10−/− mice are also severely depolarized, and their ability to remove extracellular K+ is impaired (Djukic et al., 2007), consistent with their high expression of this channel.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Deletion of gap junction proteins that link astrocytes and oligodendrocytes produces myelin pathology comparable to what occurs in Kcnj10−/− mice.
claims.source: In support of this hypothesis, deletion of gap junction proteins that link astrocytes and oligodendrocytes produces myelin pathology comparable to what occurs in Kcnj10−/− mice (Magnotti et al., 2011; Menichella et al., 2003), and heterozygote analysis indicates that there is a close genetic interaction between these connexin genes and Kir4.1 in producing myelin vacuolization (Menichella et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: There is a close genetic interaction between connexin genes and Kir4.1 in producing myelin vacuolization.
claims.source: In support of this hypothesis, deletion of gap junction proteins that link astrocytes and oligodendrocytes produces myelin pathology comparable to what occurs in Kcnj10−/− mice (Magnotti et al., 2011; Menichella et al., 2003), and heterozygote analysis indicates that there is a close genetic interaction between these connexin genes and Kir4.1 in producing myelin vacuolization (Menichella et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: The structure and function of oligodendrocytes is critically dependent on astrocytes.
claims.source: Our results emphasize that both the structure and function of oligodendrocytes is critically dependent on astrocytes, and that reactive changes in astrocytes associated with reduced Kir4.1 expression (Hinterkeuser et al., 2000; Kaiser et al., 2006; MacFarlane and Sontheimer, 1997; Pivonkova et al., 2010; Tong et al., 2014) may in turn precipitate pathological changes in myelin.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Membrane potential fluctuates predictably during the cell cycle in many cell types.
claims.source: Membrane potential fluctuates predictably during the cell cycle in many cell types (Blackiston et al., 2009; Sundelacruz et al., 2009), and previous studies indicate that K+ channels play an important role in regulating cell cycle progression in OPCs.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: K+ channels play an important role in regulating cell cycle progression in OPCs.
claims.source: Membrane potential fluctuates predictably during the cell cycle in many cell types (Blackiston et al., 2009; Sundelacruz et al., 2009), and previous studies indicate that K+ channels play an important role in regulating cell cycle progression in OPCs.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Pharmacological inhibition of delayed rectifier K+ channels in cultured OPC-like O-2A cells and OPCs in cerebellar slice cultures inhibits their proliferation and differentiation by inducing G1 arrest.
claims.source: Pharmacological inhibition of delayed rectifier K+ channels in cultured OPC-like O-2A cells and OPCs in cerebellar slice cultures inhibits their proliferation and differentiation by inducing G1 arrest (Gallo et al., 1996; Ghiani et al., 1999; Knutson et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: OPCs upregulate Kv1.3 during G1 phase of the cell cycle, and blockade of this channel prevents G1/S transition.
claims.source: Subsequent studies showed that OPCs upregulate Kv1.3 during G1 phase of the cell cycle, and blockade of this channel prevents G1/S transition (Chittajallu et al., 2002; Tegla et al., 2011), while overexpression of certain Kv1 isoforms promotes their proliferation, suggesting that OPC homeostasis is critically regulated by their membrane potential and potassium conductance.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Expression of Kir4.1 channels during astrocyte development correlates with a negative shift in RMP, cessation of cell proliferation, and increased differentiation.
claims.source: Expression of Kir4.1 channels during astrocyte development correlates with a negative shift in RMP, cessation of cell proliferation, and increased differentiation (Bordey and Sontheimer, 1997; MacFarlane and Sontheimer, 2000), and astrocytes that become proliferative after injury have lower Kir current density than non-proliferating astrocytes near the injury site (MacFarlane and Sontheimer, 1997).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Heterologous expression of Kir4.1 in glioma cells induces hyperpolarization and G1 arrest.
claims.source: In addition, heterologous expression of Kir4.1 in glioma cells induces hyperpolarization and G1 arrest, an effect nullified if cells are treated with BaCl2 to block Kir4.1 or artificially depolarized by high K+ (Higashimori and Sontheimer, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Complete removal of Kir4.1 from the CNS profoundly reduced OPC proliferation by the third postnatal week.
claims.source: However, our studies also indicate that OPCs are profoundly influenced by their environment, as complete removal of Kir4.1 from the CNS profoundly reduced their proliferation by the third postnatal week (Figure 1K).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of Ki67 immunostaining shown in Figure 1K.

claims.claim: OPCs receive synaptic input from neurons.
claims.source: OPCs receive synaptic input from neurons (Bergles et al., 2000), and the strength of these inputs is likely to be altered by changes in OPC membrane potential and membrane resistance.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: OPCs are able to regulate glutamatergic neurotransmission by shedding of cleaved NG2 ectodomains.
claims.source: It has been shown that OPCs are able to regulate glutamatergic neurotransmission by shedding of cleaved NG2 ectodomains (Sakry et al., 2014), so even subtle alterations in OPC behavior have the potential to affect synaptic communication in the brain.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Axonal Kv1 channels are abundant underneath the myelin sheath, particularly in juxtaparanodal regions.
claims.source: Axonal Kv1 channels that control repolarization and limit re-excitation by distal nodes are abundant underneath the myelin sheath, particularly in juxtaparanodal regions that are isolated from nodes of Ranvier by septate/septate-like junctions (Einheber et al., 1997; Poliak et al., 2003; Rash et al., 2016; Wang et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: A single action potential can increase the local extracellular K+ concentration in unmyelinated tissue by as much as 1 mM from a resting level of 3–3.5 mM.
claims.source: Although a single action potential can increase the local extracellular K+ concentration in unmyelinated tissue by as much as 1 mM from a resting level of 3–3.5 mM (Baylor and Nicholls, 1969; Frankenhaeuser and Hodgkin, 1956), and extracellular K+ levels can rise up to 10 mM during pathological conditions such as seizures (Moody et al., 1974), the potential for accumulation of K+ underneath myelin sheaths may be even greater due to the small peri-internodal volume and the barriers to diffusion presumed to be created by the paranodal septate junctions (Bellinger et al., 2008) (but see Hirano and Dembitzer, 1969; Hirano and Dembitzer, 1982; Rash et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Extracellular K+ levels can rise up to 10 mM during pathological conditions such as seizures.
claims.source: Although a single action potential can increase the local extracellular K+ concentration in unmyelinated tissue by as much as 1 mM from a resting level of 3–3.5 mM (Baylor and Nicholls, 1969; Frankenhaeuser and Hodgkin, 1956), and extracellular K+ levels can rise up to 10 mM during pathological conditions such as seizures (Moody et al., 1974), the potential for accumulation of K+ underneath myelin sheaths may be even greater due to the small peri-internodal volume and the barriers to diffusion presumed to be created by the paranodal septate junctions (Bellinger et al., 2008) (but see Hirano and Dembitzer, 1969; Hirano and Dembitzer, 1982; Rash et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: The Na+/K+ ATPase predominates in K+ clearance at lower activity regimes, but at higher frequencies and in situations of localized K+ release, Kir4.1 plays a more prominent role.
claims.source: Analysis of K+ dynamics arising from neuronal activity in gray matter suggest that the Na+/K+ ATPase predominates in lower activity regimes, but at higher frequencies and in situations of localized K+ release, Kir4.1 plays a more prominent role in limiting extracellular K+ accumulation (Chever et al., 2010; Larsen et al., 2014; Sibille et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Kir4.1 is concentrated within the fine processes of astrocytes that surround synapses, as well as to astrocyte endfeet that contact blood vessels.
claims.source: Kir4.1 is concentrated within the fine processes of astrocytes that surround synapses, as well as to astrocyte endfeet that contact blood vessels (Higashi et al., 2001), making it ideally situated to participate in K+ buffering.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter local K+ accumulation in the cortex after neuronal activity.
claims.source: Indeed, astrocytes appear to dominate this process in gray matter, as deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter local K+ accumulation in the cortex after neuronal activity (Battefeld et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Deletion of Kir4.1 channels from oligodendrocytes slowed both their depolarization in response to repetitive stimulation and their repolarization after the stimulus train ended.
claims.source: Our recordings in white matter revealed that deletion of Kir4.1 channels from oligodendrocytes slowed both their depolarization in response to repetitive stimulation and their repolarization after the stimulus train ended (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that these channels normally limit extracellular K+ transients induced by neuronal activity.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The membrane potential of astrocytes exhibited similarly delayed response kinetics in white matter of oKir4.1cKO mice.
claims.source: These changes were not restricted to the protected space beneath myelin, as the membrane potential of astrocytes, which closely follow the extracellular K+ concentration (Chever et al., 2010; Meeks and Mennerick, 2007; Orkand et al., 1966), exhibited similarly delayed response kinetics in white matter (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 is an important mediator of white matter extracellular K+ clearance.
claims.source: These findings indicate that oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 is an important mediator of white matter extracellular K+ clearance.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: oKir4.1cKO mice exhibited rare, but often fatal seizures.
claims.source: Mice in which Kir4.1 was removed from oligodendrocytes exhibited rare, but often fatal seizures, and a dramatic reduction in PTZ-induced seizure threshold (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: oKir4.1cKO mice exhibited a dramatic reduction in PTZ-induced seizure threshold.
claims.source: Mice in which Kir4.1 was removed from oligodendrocytes exhibited rare, but often fatal seizures, and a dramatic reduction in PTZ-induced seizure threshold (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Several spontaneously arising rodent models of epilepsy were found to have altered Kir4.1 levels.
claims.source: There is extensive evidence that Kir4.1 is a key regulator of neuronal excitability, but the involvement of oligodendrocytes in this process has not been demonstrated. Several spontaneously arising rodent models of epilepsy were found to have altered Kir4.1 levels (Harada et al., 2013; Nagao et al., 2013), and a single-nucleotide polymorphism in the Kir4.1 gene (kcnj10) was found to be responsible for differences in seizure susceptibility between C57BL6 and DBA/2 mice (Ferraro et al., 2004; Inyushin et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: A single-nucleotide polymorphism in the Kir4.1 gene (kcnj10) was found to be responsible for differences in seizure susceptibility between C57BL6 and DBA/2 mice.
claims.source: Several spontaneously arising rodent models of epilepsy were found to have altered Kir4.1 levels (Harada et al., 2013; Nagao et al., 2013), and a single-nucleotide polymorphism in the Kir4.1 gene (kcnj10) was found to be responsible for differences in seizure susceptibility between C57BL6 and DBA/2 mice (Ferraro et al., 2004; Inyushin et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Polymorphisms in KCNJ10 are risk factors for epilepsy in humans.
claims.source: In addition, polymorphisms in KCNJ10 are risk factors for epilepsy in humans (Buono et al., 2004; Dai et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015; Lenzen et al., 2005), and seizures are a prominent component of the human disorder SeSAME/EAST syndrome, which results from loss-of-function mutations in KCNJ10 (Bockenhauer et al., 2009; Scholl et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes alone is sufficient to dramatically lower seizure threshold and induce spontaneous seizures.
claims.source: However, our findings indicate that even in the absence of any structural changes to myelin, deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes alone is sufficient to dramatically lower seizure threshold and induce spontaneous seizures.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Removal of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes does not alter the excitability of cortical pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: However, recent studies indicate that removal of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes does not alter the excitability of cortical pyramidal neurons (Battefeld et al., 2016), perhaps due to the local abundance of astrocyte processes.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 knockout mice displayed significant impairments in motor behaviors.
claims.source: Oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 knockout mice also displayed significant impairments in motor behaviors (Figure 8), despite normal myelination and the absence of obvious neuronal pathology or neurodegeneration (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on behavioral testing shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Motor impairments in oKir4.1cKO mice only became apparent during high-intensity activity.
claims.source: These deficits only became apparent during high-intensity activity, consistent with an activity-dependent, rather than a neurodegenerative mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: No difference in conduction velocity was observed for myelinated or unmyelinated axon populations between control and oKir4.1cKO mice.
claims.source: To assess whether axons are functionally preserved in the absence of oligodendrocyte Kir4.1, compound action potentials (CAPs) reflecting conduction along myelinated and unmyelinated axons were recorded in the corpus callosum (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B). No difference in conduction velocity was observed for myelinated or unmyelinated axon populations between control and oKir4.1cKO mice (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The brain and spinal cord of 10-week-old oKir4.1cKO animals exhibited grossly normal white matter with ample myelin and no apparent vacuolation.
claims.source: In contrast to the striking white matter pathology exhibited by nKir4.1cKO mice, the brain and spinal cord of 10-week-old oKir4.1cKO animals exhibited grossly normal white matter with ample myelin and no apparent vacuolation (Figure 4E–F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claims.claim: There was no change in the density of EGFP+ oligodendrocytes in oKir4.1cKO mice.
claims.source: Moreover, there was no change in the density of EGFP+ oligodendrocytes (Figure 4G–H), indicating that oligodendrocyte survival was not impaired.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claims.claim: Electron micrographs demonstrated a complete absence of vacuoles or aberrant myelin in oKir4.1cKO animals.
claims.source: Electron micrographs containing cross-sections of corpus callosum from 10-week-old mice demonstrated a complete absence of vacuoles or aberrant myelin in oKir4.1cKO animals (Figure 4I–J).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on TEM data shown in Figure 4I-J.

claims.claim: There was no difference in g-ratio across all axons between control and oKir4.1cKO mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, the pattern of myelination, estimated by calculating g-ratios (diameter of axon/diameter of axon + myelin) (Figure 4K) revealed that there was no difference in g-ratio across all axons (Control: 0.743 ± 0.010 (n = 3 mice), oKir4.1cKO: 0.752 ± 0.001 (n = 3 mice), p=0.38) (Figure 4L), or in the relationship between axon diameter and g-ratio (Control: 0.16 ± 0.02 (n = 3 mice), oKir4.1cKO: 0.15 ± 0.01 (n = 3 mice), p=0.81) (Figure 4M).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of TEM data shown in Figure 4K-M.

claims.claim: Swollen or degenerating axons were completely absent from corpus callosum of oKir4.1cKO mice.
claims.source: In addition, swollen or degenerating axons were completely absent from corpus callosum of oKir4.1cKO mice (Figure 4I) and immunostaining for SMI32 (non-phosphorylated neurofilament), which is upregulated in degenerating axons (Lee et al., 2012), revealed no axonal pathology in the corpus callosum of control or oKir4.1cKO animals (n = 6 for both genotypes) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on TEM and immunostaining data shown in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A-B.

claims.claim: No difference in GFAP expression was observed between control and oKir4.1cKO animals.
claims.source: Brain sections were also immunostained for GFAP, as astrocytes become reactive and upregulate GFAP in response to neuronal degeneration (Lee et al., 2012). No difference in GFAP expression was observed between control and oKir4.1cKO animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C–D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4C-D.

claims.claim: Myelin and myelinated axons are not structurally altered as result of the selective removal of Kir4.1 channels from oligodendrocytes.
claims.source: These findings indicate that myelin and myelinated axons are not structurally altered as result of the selective removal of Kir4.1channels from oligodendrocytes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: oKir4.1cKO mice died much earlier than control littermates.
claims.source: Although oKir4.1cKO mice did not exhibit alterations in the structure of myelin or progressive disability, these animals died much earlier than control littermates (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on survival analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Nearly all (11/12) oKir4.1cKO mice exhibited tonic-clonic seizures with full hindlimb extension after being injected with PTZ, while only 1/17 control mice exhibited this level of seizure severity.
claims.source: Nearly all (11/12) oKir4.1cKO mice exhibited tonic-clonic seizures with full hindlimb extension after being injected with PTZ, while only 1/17 control mice exhibited this level of seizure severity (Figure 5B; Figure 5—video 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: 8/12 oKir4.1cKO mice and only 1/17 control mice experienced fatal seizures.
claims.source: Moreover, 8/12 oKir4.1cKO mice and only 1/17 control mice experienced fatal seizures, and oKir4.1cKO mice had a faster seizure onset (Figure 5C–D), indicating that deletion of this K+ channel from oligodendrocytes enhances neuronal excitability and increases seizure susceptibility.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5C-D.

claims.claim: oKir4.1cKO mice had a faster seizure onset than control mice.
claims.source: Moreover, 8/12 oKir4.1cKO mice and only 1/17 control mice experienced fatal seizures, and oKir4.1cKO mice had a faster seizure onset (Figure 5C–D), indicating that deletion of this K+ channel from oligodendrocytes enhances neuronal excitability and increases seizure susceptibility.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5C-D.

claims.claim: Deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes enhances neuronal excitability and increases seizure susceptibility.
claims.source: Moreover, 8/12 oKir4.1cKO mice and only 1/17 control mice experienced fatal seizures, and oKir4.1cKO mice had a faster seizure onset (Figure 5C–D), indicating that deletion of this K+ channel from oligodendrocytes enhances neuronal excitability and increases seizure susceptibility.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Extracellular K+ levels are slower to recover following neuronal stimulation in glia-specific Kir4.1 knockout mice.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that Kir4.1 is involved in buffering extracellular K+ in both gray and white matter (Bay and Butt, 2012; Chever et al., 2010; Haj-Yasein et al., 2011; Neusch et al., 2006; Sibille et al., 2014), as extracellular K+ levels are slower to recover following neuronal stimulation in glia-specific Kir4.1 knockout mice (Chever et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: Oligodendrocytes were progressively depolarized during the stimulus train due to K+ release from active axons and gradually returned to baseline after cessation of the stimulus.
claims.source: In accordance with previous studies (Battefeld et al., 2016; Yamazaki et al., 2007; 2014), oligodendrocytes were progressively depolarized during the stimulus train due to K+ release from active axons and gradually returned to baseline after cessation of the stimulus (Figure 6B–C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C) following the gradual decline in extracellular K+ levels (Battefeld et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6B-C, with citation support.

claims.claim: Oligodendrocyte depolarization occurred more slowly in oKir4.1cKO mice.
claims.source: Oligodendrocyte depolarization occurred more slowly in oKir4.1cKO mice, and the decay of membrane potential following cessation of stimulation was markedly prolonged relative to controls (Figure 6B–D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D) (corpus callosum: 11.6 ± 1.6 s (n = 15) vs. 5.9 ± 0.7 s (n = 15), p=0.0036; alveus: 9.3 ± 0.6 s (n = 16) vs. 6.3 ± 0.4 s (n = 14), p=0.0017), which was also reflected in the area under the curve (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6B-D.

claims.claim: The decay of oligodendrocyte membrane potential following cessation of stimulation was markedly prolonged in oKir4.1cKO mice relative to controls.
claims.source: Oligodendrocyte depolarization occurred more slowly in oKir4.1cKO mice, and the decay of membrane potential following cessation of stimulation was markedly prolonged relative to controls (Figure 6B–D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D) (corpus callosum: 11.6 ± 1.6 s (n = 15) vs. 5.9 ± 0.7 s (n = 15), p=0.0036; alveus: 9.3 ± 0.6 s (n = 16) vs. 6.3 ± 0.4 s (n = 14), p=0.0017), which was also reflected in the area under the curve (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6B-D.

claims.claim: Astrocyte membrane potential follows the concentration of extracellular K+ closely, due to the high permeability of their membranes to K+.
claims.source: To provide an independent assessment of extracellular K+ dynamics, we recorded the response of astrocytes in the corpus callosum and alveus of oKir4.1cKO mice (crossed to Slc1a2-EGFP mice to allow astrocyte visualization) (Figure 6F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1F). Astrocyte membrane potential follows the concentration of extracellular K+ closely, due to the high permeability of their membranes to K+ (Chever et al., 2010; Meeks and Mennerick, 2007; Orkand et al., 1966).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: A significant slowing of astrocyte decay following the end of the stimulus was observed in oKir4.1cKO mice, despite the presence of normal Kir4.1 expression by astrocytes.
claims.source: However, despite the presence of normal Kir4.1 expression by astrocytes, a significant slowing of their decay following the end of the stimulus was observed in oKir4.1cKO mice, comparable to that observed in oligodendrocytes (Figure 6G–J; Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–J).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6G-J.

claims.claim: Kir4.1 deletion from oligodendrocytes did not affect the mode (i.e. peak of the CAP) or median baseline conduction velocity of optic nerves.
claims.source: Consistent with the behavior of axons in the corpus callosum (Figure 4D), Kir4.1 deletion from oligodendrocytes did not affect the mode (i.e. peak of the CAP) or median baseline conduction velocity of the nerves (n = 5 nerves from three mice for each genotype) (Figure 7B–C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7B-C.

claims.claim: High-frequency stimulation of the optic nerve results in an increase in extracellular K+ levels and a decay of the CAP waveform.
claims.source: It is established that high-frequency stimulation of the optic nerve results in an increase in extracellular K+ levels and a decay of the CAP waveform (Bay and Butt, 2012; Ransom et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: In young Kir4.1 KO optic nerves, there is a slower restoration of the extracellular K+ concentration after stimulation.
claims.source: In young Kir4.1 KO optic nerves, there is a slower restoration of the extracellular K+ concentration after stimulation (Bay and Butt, 2012), suggesting that Kir4.1 plays an important role in K+ clearance in this tissue.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claims.claim: The CAP waveform in oKir4.1cKO optic nerves took significantly longer to recover after stimulation ended.
claims.source: Although oKir4.1cKO nerves exhibited a similar reduction in peak amplitude during stimulation, the CAP waveform in these nerves took significantly longer to recover after stimulation ended (Figure 7E–F).

results.result: CNS-wide deletion of Kir4.1 (nKir4.1cKO mice) causes severe phenotypes including early mortality, ataxia, tremor, widespread myelin vacuolization, and oligodendrocyte depolarization, but does not impair oligodendrocyte generation or maturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C43 collectively demonstrate that CNS-wide Kir4.1 deletion produces severe pathology (vacuolization, depolarization) without preventing oligodendrocyte development. The data include immunostaining (C36, C37, C38), electrophysiology (C41, C42), and proliferation assays (C39, C40), all supporting the conclusion that oligodendrocytes form and mature despite profound structural and functional changes.

results.result: Deletion of Kir4.1 from OPCs (pKir4.1cKO mice) causes profound depolarization (~20 mV) and ~10-fold increase in membrane resistance, indicating that Kir4.1 dominates OPC resting conductance.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 are supported by electrophysiological recordings showing loss of Ba2+-sensitive inward currents in 76% of OPCs, significant depolarization, and increased membrane resistance. The data directly demonstrate Kir4.1's role in setting OPC membrane properties, with appropriate controls and statistical analysis.

results.result: Despite profound changes in membrane properties, deletion of Kir4.1 from OPCs does not alter their density, proliferation, or differentiation into oligodendrocytes in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are supported by comprehensive fate-mapping and BrdU incorporation studies showing no differences in OPC density, proliferation rates, or differentiation between control and pKir4.1cKO mice. This surprising finding is well-documented with quantitative immunohistochemistry and appropriate statistical comparisons.

results.result: Selective deletion of Kir4.1 from mature oligodendrocytes (oKir4.1cKO mice) does not alter their membrane properties, myelin structure, or baseline axonal conduction velocity.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 and C130-C134 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: qPCR confirming selective deletion (C130, C131), electrophysiology showing no change in membrane properties (C132, C133), immunostaining and TEM showing normal myelin (C57), and CAP recordings showing normal conduction velocity (C58). The BaCl2 experiments (C134) suggest compensation by other K+ channels.

results.result: Oligodendrocyte-specific Kir4.1 deletion does not cause myelin pathology, axonal degeneration, or reactive astrocytosis, as demonstrated by normal myelin structure, g-ratios, and absence of degenerative markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C99 are supported by comprehensive structural analysis including CAP recordings (C92), immunostaining (C93, C94, C98), TEM (C95), g-ratio analysis (C96), and markers of degeneration (C97). The data convincingly demonstrate that oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 is not required for myelin maintenance, contrasting with CNS-wide deletion.

results.result: Deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes impairs K+ clearance in white matter, as evidenced by slower depolarization and prolonged recovery of both oligodendrocytes and astrocytes following repetitive axonal stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 and C106-C110 are supported by electrophysiological recordings in corpus callosum and alveus showing significantly prolonged decay times (~2-fold increase) in both oligodendrocytes and astrocytes. The fact that astrocytes (which retain Kir4.1) also show delayed kinetics (C110) strongly supports impaired extracellular K+ clearance rather than cell-autonomous effects.

results.result: Oligodendrocyte-specific Kir4.1 deletion causes spontaneous seizures, dramatically reduced PTZ-induced seizure threshold, and early mortality.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84 and C100-C104 are supported by survival analysis (C100), PTZ challenge experiments showing 11/12 oKir4.1cKO mice reaching maximum seizure severity vs. 1/17 controls (C101), and 8/12 fatal seizures in knockouts vs. 1/17 in controls (C102). The data provide strong evidence that oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 is sufficient to regulate seizure susceptibility.

results.result: Oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 deletion does not affect baseline optic nerve conduction velocity but significantly delays recovery of compound action potentials following high-frequency (100 Hz) and lower-frequency (20 Hz) stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C117 are supported by optic nerve CAP recordings showing normal baseline conduction (C111) but significantly prolonged recovery after both 100 Hz and 20 Hz stimulation (C114-C116). The data demonstrate that oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 is important for activity-dependent K+ clearance across physiological and pathophysiological frequency ranges.

results.result: Oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 knockout mice show activity-dependent motor deficits, with normal baseline locomotion but impaired performance on rotarod and running wheel tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 and C118-C124 are supported by behavioral testing showing normal open field activity (C118) but significantly impaired rotarod performance (C119) and reduced running wheel distance/speed (C120-C123). The activity-dependent nature of deficits is consistent with impaired K+ clearance during high-intensity neuronal activity.

results.result: Background knowledge establishing that Kir4.1 is broadly expressed in CNS glia, plays roles in K+ homeostasis and membrane potential regulation, and its dysfunction is associated with seizures, myelin pathology, and human genetic disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C34 represent established knowledge from prior literature, appropriately cited throughout. These claims provide essential context for the study but are not novel findings. They are consistently supported by the cited references and represent accepted knowledge in the field.

results.result: Additional background knowledge and discussion points regarding OPC biology, K+ channel function, cell cycle regulation, myelin structure, and prior studies on Kir4.1 function.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C129 (selected) represent additional established knowledge and discussion points that contextualize the findings. These are appropriately cited and provide important background for interpreting the results, but are not novel experimental findings from this study.

results.result: The authors conclude that oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 plays an important role in white matter K+ homeostasis and that selective loss from oligodendrocytes is sufficient to impair K+ clearance and promote seizures.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 and C88 represent the main conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the collective evidence from K+ clearance experiments (C80-C82), seizure susceptibility studies (C83-C84, C100-C104), and the absence of structural defects (C92-C99). The conclusions logically follow from the experimental data.
